div.head: Introduction
div.p: The Cyclic Executive Rate Monotonic Scheduling Earliest Deadline First Scheduling Other Kinds of Synchronization Mutual exclusion is not the only kind of synchronization of importance.
Condition synchronization is another significant requirement.

It is needed when a process can perform an operation in a meaningful way only after another process has itself taken another action, or is in some specific state. When a set of producer and consumer processes share a circular memory buffer, a consumer must not attempt to take data from the buffer if the buffer is empty.
Symmetrically, a producer must not attempt to store data into the buffer if the buffer is full.
Moreover, mutual exclusion is still needed so that, for example, multiple producers operating concurrently do not corrupt the "next free slot" pointer of the buffer.

div.head: Concurrent Programming and Real-Time
div.p: In any concurrent program, the exact order in which processes execute is not specified.
According to the concurrent programming theory, synchronization primitives are used to enforce the local ordering constraints needed to ensure that the results of the program are correct.

For example, a semaphore can be used to ensure mutual exclusion, thus avoiding race conditions, when appropriate. Despite these constraints, the general behavior of the program still exhibits significant non-determinism due to interleaving.

div.head: Timings Come into Place
div.p: Although the concurrent program's output will be identical for all the possible interleavings (provided it is correct), the timing behavior may vary considerably.
Hence, for example, if one of the concurrent processes has a tight deadline, only some of the interleavings will meet its temporal requirements, even if its results will have the right value anyway.

A real-time system needs to further restrict the non-determinism found within concurrent systems, because some interleavings that are correct with respect to results can be unacceptable with respect to timings. The Role of the Scheduling Model
The main goal of a real-time scheduling model is to ensure that a concurrent program is correct with respect to timings, too.
In order to do this, it provides two main features:
1. A scheduling algorithm for ordering the use of system resources, the processor(s) in particular.
2. A means of predicting the worst-case behavior of the system, with respect to timings, when that scheduling algorithm is applied.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The Cyclic Executive Rate Monotonic Scheduling Earliest Deadline First Scheduling General-Purpose vs. Real-Time Scheduling
When choosing a scheduling algorithm, it is often necessary to look for a compromise between optimizing the mean system performance and its determinism.
Since they are less concerned with determinism, most general-purpose scheduling algorithms emphasize fairness and efficiency, and optimize the system throughput.
On the other hand, real-time scheduling algorithms must put the emphasis on timings, even if this entails a greater overhead and the mean performance of the system becomes worse.
The scheduling algorithms can take advantage of the greater amount of information that, on most real-time systems, is available on the processes to be executed.

div.head: A Simple Process Model
div.p: Analyzing an arbitrarily complex concurrent program to predict its worst-case timing behavior is very difficult, hence it is necessary to impose some restrictions on the structure of real-time concurrent programs. The most basic model has the following characteristics:
1. The application consists of a fixed number of processes.
2. All processes are periodic, with known periods.

3. The processes are completely independent of each other. 4. All processes have hard deadlines, and the deadline of each process is equal to its period. 5. All processes have known and fixed worst-case execution times. 6. All overheads (e.g. context switch times), are negligible.

div.head: Model Generalizations
div.p: The basic model just introduced has a number of shortcomings, and will be generalized to make it more suitable to describe real-world systems.
In particular:
The hypothesis of independence among processes is somewhat contrary to the motivations of concurrent systems, in which processes must interact with one another.

The deadline of a process is not always related to its period, and is often shorter than it. Some processes are sporadic, that is, they are executed when an external event, for example an alarm, occurs.

div.head: Further Generalizations
div.p: For some applications and hardware architectures, scheduling and context switch times are far from being negligible.
The behavior of some non-deterministic hardware components, for example caches, must sometimes be taken into account.

Real-time systems may sometimes be overloaded, a critical situation in which the computational demand exceeds the system capacity during a certain time interval, so that not all processes can meet their deadline.

Basic Notation
div.p: A periodic real-time process is called a task and is denoted by τ i .
The j-th instance of a task is sometimes called a job; accordingly, τ i,j denotes the j-th instance of the i-th task.
T i is the period of task τ i . D i is the relative deadline of task τ i . d i,j is the absolute deadline of the j-th instance of task τ i .

C i is the worst-case execution time of task τ i . R i is the worst-case response time of task τ i . The actual completion time -also known as response time -may be longer due, for example, to preemption.
Although relative deadlines (with respect to the task release time) are known and fixed for any given task, absolute deadlines depend on the task instance.

div.head: Basics of the Cyclic Executive
div.p: The cyclic executive, also known as timeline scheduling or cyclic scheduling, is still one of the most widely used real-time scheduling methods.
It is assumed that the basic model just introduced holds, hence there is a fixed set of periodic tasks.
It is possible to lay out offline a complete schedule such that its repeated execution will cause all tasks to run at their correct rate and to meet their deadline.

div.head: Major and Minor Cycles
div.p: The complete table, known as the major cycle, is typically split into a number of slices called minor cycles, with a fixed duration.
During execution, the cyclic executive switches from one minor cycle to another with the help of a periodic clock interrupt.
As a consequence, only the activation of the tasks at the beginning of each minor cycle is synchronized with the real elapsed time.

On the other hand, all the tasks belonging to the same minor cycle are simply activated in sequence. . . . it can be scheduled on a single processor system, with a major cycle of 100 ms and a minor cycle of 25 ms, as follows:

div.head: Implementation of a Cyclic Executive
div.p: Provided an interrupt source with a 25 ms period is available, and the intwait function waits for an interrupt from this source, we can code the cyclic executive as:

while(1) { intwait(); proc1(...); proc2(...); proc3(...); intwait(); proc1(...); proc2(...); proc4(...); proc5(...); intwait(); proc1(...); proc2(...); proc3(...); intwait(); proc1(...); proc2(...); proc4(...); } where proc1, . . . proc5 are the procedures that contain the code of tasks τ 1 , . . . τ 5 , respectively.

div.head: Choice of the Minor Cycle Length
div.p: The minor cycle period is the smallest timing reference of the cyclic executive.
All task periods must be an integer multiple of the minor cycle period.
Otherwise, the schedule would be unable to guarantee that the tasks will be executed at their proper rate.

div.head: Optimum minor cycle length
div.p: It is easy to show that the minor cycle period must be equal to the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) of the periods of the tasks to be scheduled.

div.head: Choice of the Major Cycle Length
div.p: By definition, the major cycle period is the maximum period that can be accommodated without secondary schedules. Secondary schedules are procedures that are called at each major cycle and, in turn, call a secondary procedure every n major cycles. Therefore, secondary schedules may be useful to accommodate tasks with long periods without enlarging the major cycle length too much.

div.head: Choice of the major cycle length
div.p: When secondary schedules are not used, the major cycle period must be equal to the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of the periods of the tasks to be scheduled.

div.head: Properties of the Cyclic Executive
div.p: No actual processes exist at run-time, because the minor cycles are just a sequence of procedure calls.
These procedures share a common address space, hence they implicitly share data.
If we neglect interrupt handlers and only consider a single processor system, the shared data does not need to be protected, because concurrent access is not possible.

div.head: Properties of the Cyclic Executive
div.p: Once a suitable cyclic executive has been constructed, its implementation is straightforward and efficient, because no scheduling activity takes place at run-time and overheads are very low.
The sequence of tasks in the schedule is always the same, and can be easily visualized.
The existence of a cyclic executive that meets the timing requirements of a set of tasks is a "proof by construction" of its schedulability.

div.head: Shortcomings of the Cyclic Executive
div.p: The cyclic executive "processes" cannot be protected from each other, as regular processes are.
It is difficult to incorporate sporadic processes efficiently without changing the task sequence.
When the periods of the tasks are mutually prime, the cyclic executive scheduling table will be large.
Tasks with long periods are also problematic, because secondary schedules are tricky. For example, their worst-case execution time is far from the mean execution time.

div.head: Tasks with Sizable Execution Times
div.p: Any task with an execution time greater than the minor cycle time (and possibly other tasks as well, to avoid "monopolizing" a minor cycle) will need to be split into a number of smaller procedures.

The split may cut across the structure of the code in a way that has nothing to do with the structure of the code itself. The schedule is sensitive to any change in the task characteristics, above all their periods, which requires the entire scheduling sequence to be reconstructed from scratch.
In addition, building a cyclic executive is mathematically hard by itself.

div.head: Constructing a Cyclic Executive is Hard
div.p: The construction of a cyclic executive can be put into analogy with the classical bin packing problem.
With that problem, items of varying sizes (in just one dimension, like the task instances in this case) must be placed in the minimum number of bins (the minor cycles) so that no bin is overfull.
The analogy does not take into account secondary schedules and the necessity of splitting "long" tasks.
The bin-packing problem is known to be NP-hard.
For sizable problems, sub-optimal schemes, based on heuristics, must be used.

div.head: Process-Based Scheduling
div.p: With the cyclic executive approach, the notion of process is not preserved during execution.
An alternative approach is to support process execution directly, as is normally done in general-purpose operating systems.
In this case, the process to be executed at any one time is determined by using one or more scheduling attributes.
With this approach, the process becomes the unit of scheduling.

div.head: Scheduling Approaches
div.p: Assuming that process scheduling is being used, there are still many different scheduling approaches. Among them, we will consider:
1. Fixed-Priority Scheduling (FPS): each process has a fixed, static priority which is computed offline, before run-time. The ready processes are then scheduled according to their priority.

2. Earliest Deadline First (EDF): the ready processes are executed in the order determined by their absolute deadlines, the highest priority process being the one with the nearest deadline. Since absolute deadlines are computed at run-time, the priority assignment is dynamic. In a preemptive scheduling scheme, if a high-priority process becomes ready during the execution of a lower priority one, there will be an immediate switch to the higher-priority process.
Alternatively, if the scheme is non-preemptive, the lower-priority process will be allowed to complete.
+ Preemptive schemes make higher-priority processes more reactive.

+ They also prevent rogue processes from "monopolizing" the CPU. In a preemptive scheduling scheme, if a high-priority process becomes ready during the execution of a lower priority one, there will be an immediate switch to the higher-priority process.
Alternatively, if the scheme is non-preemptive, the lower-priority process will be allowed to complete.
-Preemption is responsible for most race conditions.
-For example, the cyclic executive avoids most race conditions by executing its tasks in a well-defined sequence and without preemption. The Rate Monotonic Scheduler
The basic process model just introduced is being used.
Tasks have a static priority.
They are scheduled preemptively and according to their priority.
There is only one processor.

div.head: An optimum priority assignment scheme
div.p: Under these hypotheses, there exists a simple, optimum priority assignment scheme, due to Liu and Layland (1973) and known as Rate Monotonic (RM).

div.head: RM Priority Assignment
div.p: Each task is assigned a (fixed) priority that is inversely proportional to its period: the shorter the period, the higher the priority.

This assignment is optimum in the sense that if any task set can be scheduled using a preemptive, fixed-priority scheduler. . . . . . then the same task set can also be scheduled using the rate monotonic priority assignment. task τ 1 (which has the smallest period) will have the highest priority, followed by τ 3 and τ 2 , in that order.

div.head: Caution!
div.p: Priorities are often expressed by integers, but there is no general agreement on whether higher values represent higher priorities or the other way round. Simulating the Schedule (I)

In order to better understand how a scheduler (the rate monotonic scheduler in this case) works, and to draw some conclusions about its characteristics, we can build the corresponding scheduling diagram.
To be meaningful, the simulation must be carried out for an amount of time that is "long enough" to cover all possible phase relations among the tasks.
In general, the right amount of time is the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of the task periods.
Since we do not have any additional information about the tasks, we also assume that all tasks are simultaneously released at t = 0.

div.head: Definitions
div.p: According to the simple process model, the relative deadline of a task is equal to its period, that is, D i = T i ∀i.

Hence, for each task instance, the absolute deadline is the time of its next release, that is, d i,j = r i,j+1 . We say that there is an overflow at time t if t is the deadline of a job that misses the deadline. A scheduling algorithm is feasible for a given set of task if they are scheduled so that no overflows ever occur.

div.head: Definition of critical instant and critical time zone
div.p: A critical instant for a task is an instant at which the release of the task will produce the largest response time.
A critical time zone for a task is the interval between a critical instant and the end of the task response. Where Are the Critical Instants?
Theorem (Liu and Layland, 1973) A critical instant for any task occurs whenever it is released simultaneously with the release of all higher priority tasks.
This theorem is useful for scheduling analysis, because it describes a situation that leads to the worst-case response time of a given set of tasks.
It is valid for any fixed-priority scheduling algorithm (not just Rate Monotonic). The Earliest Deadline First Scheduler Can we do any better than RM?
We can do better than RM if we abandon the hypothesis of using static priorities.
The basic process model is still being used. Task priorities are assigned dynamically.
They are scheduled preemptively.
There is only one processor.

div.head: An optimum scheduling algorithm
div.p: Under these hypotheses, there exists an optimum scheduling algorithm, due to Liu and Layland (1973) and known as Earliest Deadline First (EDF).

div.head: EDF Priority Assignment
div.p: The EDF algorithm selects tasks according to their absolute deadlines. Namely, at each instant, tasks with earlier deadlines will receive higher priorities.
The absolute deadline d i,j of the j-th instance of task τ i is:
div.formula: d i,j = Φ i + jT i + D i ,
div.p: where Φ i is the phase of τ i , that is, the release time of its first instance (for which j = 0).
Hence, the priority of each task is assigned dynamically, instance by instance, but the priority of each instance (job) is still fixed.

div.head: FPS Versus EDF
div.p: FPS is easier to implement than EDF, as the scheduling attribute (priority) is static.
EDF requires a more complex run-time system, which will typically have a higher overhead.
During overload situations, the behavior of FPS is easier to predict (the lower-priority processes will miss their deadlines first).
EDF is less predictable, and can experience a domino effect in which a large number of tasks unnecessarily miss their deadline.
As for processor utilization, EDF is always able to exploit the full processor capacity, whereas FPS in the worst case does not.

div.head: Schedulability Tests
div.p: Our goal is to define several schedulability tests for RM and EDF which, from very simple calculations based on the tasks' period and execution time, state either a necessary or a sufficient schedulability condition (or both) for a given task set.
In the following, unless otherwise specified, we will assume that the basic process model is acceptable and being used.
Moreover, we assume that a single-processor system is being used.

Of course, sufficient (but not necessary) schedulability tests will not be exact, but somewhat "pessimistic". Processor Utilization Factor Definition Given a set of N periodic tasks Γ = {τ i , . . . , τ N } the processor utilization factor U is the fraction of processor time spent in the execution of the task set.
Since C i /T i is the fraction of processor time spent executing task τ i , the utilization for the whole set of N tasks is:
div.formula: U = N i=1 C i T i
div.p: The processor utilization factor is a measure of the computational load imposed on the processor by a given task set.

div.head: Full Utilization
div.p: Given a task set Γ, its processor utilization factor can be increased by increasing the execution times C i of the tasks.

For a given scheduling algorithm A, there exists a maximum value of U below which the task set Γ is schedulable, but for which any increase in the C i of any of the tasks in the task set will make it no longer schedulable.

div.head: Full Utilization
div.p: The limit depends on the task set Γ (namely, on the relationships among tasks' periods), and on the scheduling algorithm A.

div.head: Definition
div.p: A task set Γ is said to fully utilize the processor with a given scheduling algorithm A if:
It is schedulable by A, but. . . any increase in the C i of any of its tasks will make it no longer schedulable.
The corresponding upper bound of the utilization factor is denoted as U ub (Γ, A).

div.head: Least Upper Bound
div.p: It is interesting (and useful) to ask how large the utilization factor can be, in order to guarantee the schedulability of any task set Γ by a given scheduling algorithm A.
In order to do this, we must determine the minimum value of U ub (Γ, A) over all task sets Γ which fully utilize the processor.

div.head: Definition
div.p: For a given scheduling algorithm A, the least upper bound U lub (A) of the utilization factor is defined as:
div.formula: U lub (A) = min Γ U ub (Γ, A) ISIE 2010 -4

Namely, this is possible only if the task periods are suitably related.

div.head: Necessary Schedulability Test Theorem
div.p: If the processor utilization factor U of a task set Γ is greater than one (that is, if U > 1), then the task set is not schedulable, regardless of the scheduling algorithm.
Recalling the definition of U for a set of N tasks Γ = {τ 1 , . . . , τ N }, the necessary condition can be written as:
div.formula: N i=1 C i T i ≤ 1 ISIE 2010 -4

div.head: Extension to Multiprocessor Systems
div.p: The theorem can be extended to multiprocessor systems; in this case, for M CPUs, the necessary condition becomes:
div.formula: N i=1 C i T i ≤ M
div.p: This kind of extension seems intuitive, but it is rarely possible.

For example, the rate monotonic scheduling is provably optimum for single processor systems, but is not necessarily optimum for multiprocessor systems. We already showed that the RM priority assignment is optimum among all other static priority assignment schemes for single processor systems under the basic process model.

From this, we will derive a sufficient schedulability test for RM so that, if a given task set Γ satisfies it, its schedulability will be guaranteed by using RM.

div.head: Observation
div.p: The utilization-based tests for RM are quite simple and useful, but have several significant drawbacks. A different, more sophisticated approach is needed to cope with these limitations. (Audsley et al., 1992) To find an exact (necessary and sufficient) schedulability test for any fixed priority assignment scheme, the exact interleaving of higher-priority tasks must be analyzed, individually, for each task.
The test is performed in two stages:
1. An analytical method is used to predict the worst-case response time of each task.
2. These values are then compared with the corresponding task deadlines to assess whether all tasks meet their deadline or not.

div.head: Conclusion of the Analysis
div.p: The worst-case response time R i is individually calculated for each task τ i ∈ Γ.
If, at any point, either a diverging succession is encountered or R i > D i for some i, then Γ is not schedulable, because τ i misses its deadline.
Else, Γ is schedulable and the worst-case response time is known for all tasks.

div.head: Additional Remarks
div.p: Preemptive, fixed-priority scheduling, with the DM priority ordering, can adequately deal with process systems in which D i ≤ T i .
For EDF, the simple U-based necessary and sufficient schedulability test is no longer valid in this case.
The response time analysis method can indeed be applied to EDF, but is considerably more complex that for FPS.
The response time analysis method for FPS has proved its effectiveness when dealing with an extended process model, hence it has been used as a starting point for further extensions.

div.head: Further Extension of the Process Model
div.p: The basic process model provides a simple framework for schedulability analysis, but embodies several "unrealistic" assumptions.
The assumption D i = T i has already been replaced by D i ≤ T i to support, for example, sporadic processes as well as periodic processes.

div.head: Process interaction is useful
div.p: Another inconvenient assumption is the need for processes to be independent. Process interaction is needed in most real-world applications.
The interaction leads to the possibility of a process being blocked until some future event occurs.

div.head: Process Interaction
div.p: In a real-time system, process interaction must be designed with great care, above all when the tasks being synchronized have different priorities.
In fact, when a process is waiting for a lower-priority process to complete some required computation, the process priority scheme is, in some sense, being undermined.

div.head: Process Interaction
div.p: This happens, for example, when processes access shared resources by means of a critical region protected by a mutual exclusion semaphore: if a lower-priority process is inside its critical region, any higher-priority process wanting to enter the critical region must wait until it exits.

div.head: Priority inversion
div.p: This phenomenon is called priority inversion and can have adverse effects on schedulability. To enter the critical region, H must be prepared to wait up to the maximum time needed by L to execute its critical region. This is a direct consequence of the mutual exclusion necessary to access the shared resources in a safe way.
2. On the other hand, the blocking time of H cannot be bounded by the worst-case execution time, or duration, of the critical region of L in the general case:
The blocking time also depends on the worst-case execution time of M, a process which has "nothing to do" with H and L.

Any other intermediate-priority process which can preempt L will also have an effect on the blocking time of H. This can be obtained by either disabling interrupts or locking the scheduler within critical regions.
In other words, it is "as if" a process inside a critical region implicitly assumed the highest possible priority in the system.

div.head: Limited applicability
div.p: However, this is only appropriate for very short critical regions, because it causes unnecessary blocking. A more sophisticated approach is needed in the general case.

div.head: Priority Inheritance Protocol
div.p: The priority inheritance protocol (Sha, Rajkumar and Lehoczky, 1990) offers a straightforward solution to the problem of unbounded priority inversion.
The basic idea behind it is to dynamically increase the priority of the processes that cause blocking.
In particular, when a process L is blocking one or more higher-priority processes H 1 , . . . , H n , it temporarily inherits the highest priority of the blocked processes.

This prevents any intermediate-priority process M from preempting L and thus prolonging the blocking experienced by the higher-priority processes. H tries to enter the critical region by means of P(mutex): it still waits (because L is already inside), but it also transmits its priority to L → L runs in place of M.

div.head: Kinds of Blocking
div.p: The introduction of the priority inheritance protocol makes the concept of blocking more complex. There are now two distinct kinds of blocking:

Push-through blocking. This kind of blocking is a consequence of the priority inheritance protocol, occurs when an intermediate-priority process (M in the previous example) cannot run because a lower-priority job (L) has temporarily inherited a higher priority, and can affect even processes which does not use any shared resource. Nevertheless, it is necessary to avoid unbounded priority inversion.

div.head: Properties of the Priority Inheritance Protocol
div.p: The maximum blocking time that each process may experience is bounded.
It is possible to define several algorithms to compute the maximum blocking time for each process, in order to analyze the schedulability of a periodic task set.
As usual, these algorithms entail a trade-off between the tightness of the bound they compute and their complexity.

div.head: Nesting of Critical Regions
div.p: For simplicity, in the following discussion the fact that critical regions can be nested into each other will be neglected.
Under the assumption that critical regions are properly nested, the set of critical regions belonging to the same process is partially ordered by region inclusion.
For each process, it is possible to restrict the attention to the set of maximal critical regions, that is, the regions which are not included within any other.
It can be shown that most results discussed in the following are still valid even if only maximal critical regions are taken into account, unless otherwise specified.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The priority ceiling protocols

All of these issues are addressed by the priority ceiling protocols, also proposed by Sha, Rajkumar and Lehoczky (1990); in particular, we will discuss the original priority ceiling protocol and its immediate variant. Both have the following properties:
1. A high-priority process can be blocked at most once during its execution by lower-priority processes.
2. They prevent transitive blocking.
3. They prevent deadlock.
4. Mutually exclusive access to resources is ensured by the protocols themselves.

div.head: Basic Idea
div.p: The basic idea of this method is to extend the priority inheritance protocol with an additional rule for granting lock requests to a free semaphore.

The protocol ensures that if process L holds a resource, and it could lead to the blocking of an higher-priority process H, then no other resource that could also block H is allowed to be acquired by any process other than L.

div.head: Basic Idea
div.p: Hence, a process can be delayed not only by attempting to lock a busy semaphore, but also when granting a lock to a free semaphore could lead to multiple blocking on higher-priority processes.

This form of blocking, that the priority ceiling protocol introduces in addition to direct and push-through blocking, is called ceiling blocking. The underlying hypotheses are the same as those of the priority inheritance protocol.
Each resource (semaphore) has a static ceiling value defined, the maximum priority of all processes that use it.

As in the priority inheritance protocol, each process has a dynamic active priority that is the maximum of its initial priority and any it inherits due to it blocking higher-priority processes. The immediate priority ceiling protocol takes a more straightforward approach and raises the priority of a process to the priority ceiling associated with a resource as soon as the process acquires it, rather than only when the process is blocking a higher-priority process. Hence, it is defined as follows:
Each process has a static, initial priority assigned.

Each resource (semaphore) has a static ceiling defined, this is the maximum priority of all processes that use it. Given that a value for the worst-case blocking time B i that a task τ i can suffer has been obtained, its worst-case response time R i can be redefined to take B i into account as:

div.p: This formulation is now pessimistic (still sufficient, but no longer necessary) because a process does not necessarily suffer its worst-case blocking time. The general-purpose algorithms to cope with priority inversion have a non-negligible overhead.
For a specific case, their effect on the average and worst-case response time of the processes involved can be less than optimal.
Hence. . . Some Authors suggest to avoid attacking the priority inversion problem at the operating system level, and work at the application level instead, by means of:
• Accurate design.
• Temporary and explicit modification of process' priorities.
• Adoption of lock and wait-free data structures.

div.head: Sources of Delay
div.p: As we saw before, the naive usage of lock-based object sharing may result in unbounded priority inversion.
The overheads associated with the traditional techniques that deal with this issue can be excessive.
In addition, some hardware and software components introduce delays that make C(k ) inherently hard to predict precisely on modern systems. For example:

Page faults (on demand-paging systems) Lock-Free Objects Definition Given a system of processes J = {J 1 , . . . J n } wishing to access a shared object S, the implementation of S is lock-free (sometimes called nonblocking) if: some process J i ∈ J must complete an operation on S after the system J takes a finite number of steps.
Guarantees that some process J i will always make progress, regardless of arbitrary delays or halting failures of other processes in J.
Rules out the use of critical sections.

div.head: Underlying Hypotheses Hardware-based atomicity
div.p: There are basic units of data, called digits, which can be read and written by means of indivisible, atomic operations.
In other words, it is assumed that the underlying hardware automatically sequences concurrent operations at the level of a single digit.
However, a digit might contain just a single data bit, hence this hypothesis is not overly restrictive.

For example, many shared-memory multiprocessor systems provide this kind of support for single memory words. It is assumed that two distinct processes cannot concurrently modify v (there is only one writer).
Let v [0] denote the initial value of v. This value is written by an operation which precedes all read operations.
Let v [1] , v [2] , . . . denote the successive values of v over time.
Each write operation to v begins with v equal to v [i] (for some i ≥ 0) and ends with v equal to v [i+1] .
Real Informal Discussion of Correctness Due to the read/write order, the reader always obtains a value of v2 less than or equal to the last value just (or being) written.
For the same reason, the value obtained by reading v1 is always greater than or equal to the last value just (or being) written.
If the reader obtains the same value from reading v2 and v1, it also read a single, consistent version of the shared data.
Otherwise, it might have obtained an inconsistent value, and it retries the operation. A reader may retry a read even if it already obtained a consistent version of D.

div.head: Additional Remarks
div.p: The Lamport's writer is wait-free, because it always completes an operation after taking a finite number of steps.
However, it can interfere with concurrent read operations, forcing them to be retried. The number of tries required to successfully complete a read is unbounded.
The extreme case happens then the writer halts partway along the update. Any subsequent read operation will then be retried forever (because it will always be
For this reason, the Lamport's algorithm is lock-free, but not wait-free.

div.head: Motivation
div.p: Ad-hoc techniques, such as Lamport's algorithms, have successfully been used as building blocks to construct more complex lock-free objects.
However, they may be difficult to understand and to prove correct.
In other words, they are not general enough for widespread adoption.
"A practical methodology should permit a programmer to design, say, a correct lock-free priority queue without ending up with a publishable result" (M. Herlihy). Herlihy's Approach
An arbitrary lock-free object is designed in two steps:
1. The programmer implements the object as a stylized, sequential program, with no explicit synchronization, following certain simple conventions.
2. The sequential implementation is transformed into a lock-free or wait-free implementation by surrounding its code with a general synchronization and memory management layer.
It can be proved that if the sequential implementation is correct, the transformed implementation is correct as well. Underlying Hardware Support
Besides the usual atomic read and write operations on shared variables, the Herlihy's approach requires hardware support for:
A load_linked operation, which copies a shared variable into a local variable.
A subsequent store_conditional operation, which stores back a new value into the shared variable only if no other process has modified the same variable in the meantime.
Otherwise, store_conditional fails without doing anything.
In either case, store_conditional returns a success/failure indication.
store_conditional is permitted to fail (with a low probability) even if the variable has not been modified. The Lock-Free Transformation, Basic Technique (II)
It is assumed that all processes share a variable that holds a pointer to the current version of the shared object. Each process acts on the object by means of the following four steps:
1. It reads the pointer using load_linked.
2. It copies the indicated version into another block.
3. It performs the sequential operation on the copy.
4. It tries to move the pointer from the old version to the new by means of store_conditional.

If step 4 fails, the process restarts from step 1. Each iteration of these steps is called an attempt. Properties 1. The linearizability of the concurrent implementation is straightforward to prove: the order in which operations appear to happen is the same as the (total) order of their final, successful execution of store_conditional.

2. If store_conditional cannot fail "spontaneously", the concurrent implementation is lock-free because at least one out of every n attempts (where n is the number of processes in the system) must succeed.

div.head: Corollaries
div.p: Under the hypotheses of the theorem, it is possible to check whether or not a given, fixed priority assignment scheme will yield a feasible scheduling algorithm, without simulating it for the LCM of the periods.
If all tasks fulfill their deadlines when they are released simultaneously, that is, at their critical instant, then the scheduling algorithm is feasible.
This is a sufficient feasibility condition because, depending on the relative phases of the tasks, the critical instant may never occur in the actual schedule.

div.head: Underlying Hypotheses
div.p: Each process has a fixed initial (or baseline) priority and an active priority which is set dynamically and is initially set to the initial priority.
Processes are scheduled by a fixed-priority scheduler on a single-processor system, that is, if several processes are ready to run, the highest-priority job will be run.
Processes with the same priority are executed according to a First Come, First Served (FCFS) discipline.
Semaphore wait queues are ordered by active priority.
There is not any other source of blocking, for example I/O operations, in the system.

div.head: Protocol Definition
div.p: When a process H tries to enter a critical region which is "busy" it blocks, but it also transmits its active priority to the process L which is blocking it, if the active priority of L is lower than H's.
Hence, L will execute the rest of its critical region with a priority equal to the inherited priority. In general, a process inherits the highest priority of the processes it blocks.
When a process L exits a critical region, its active priority returns back to the nominal priority if it does not block any other process.
Otherwise (critical regions can be nested) its active priority is set to the highest priority of the processes it still blocks. Worst-Case Blocking Time

div.head: Theorem
div.p: Let K be the total number of semaphores (resources) in the system.
If critical regions cannot be nested, the worst-case blocking time experienced by each activation of task τ i under the priority inheritance protocol is bounded by B i :

div.head: Comments
div.p: This algorithm is not optimal for the priority inheritance protocol, but it is an acceptable compromise between the tightness of the bound it calculates and its computational complexity.

Better algorithms exist, and are able to provide a tighter bound of the worst-case blocking time, but they are considerably more complex. Let K be the total number of semaphores (resources) in the system. The worst-case blocking time experienced by each activation of task τ i under the priority ceiling protocol is bounded by B i :

div.head: Comments
div.p: The benefit of the priority ceiling protocol is that a high-priority process can only be blocked once per activation by any lower-priority process.
The price to be paid is that, informally speaking, more processes may experience this block, on average. Uncontrolled access to a shared object may lead to corruption of data (race condition).
Object access is traditionally implemented by means of critical sections.
A mutual exclusion mechanism, a semaphore for instance, ensures than only one process at a time is allowed to access the object.

div.head: Lock-Based Object Sharing
div.p: In lock-based object sharing, a process wishing to access a shared object must obey the following protocol:
1. Acquire a lock of some sort 2. Access the shared object

div.head: Release the lock
div.p: While a process holds a lock, any other process contending for the same lock is enforced to wait.

If the process holding the lock is delayed (or halted), the other processes will be unable to progress (possibly forever). If any process J i acquires the lock, enters the critical section, and halts without releasing the lock. . . . . . regardless of which steps the system J takes, and of the number of such steps, none of the processes will complete its operation.

All processes will wait forever to acquire the lock, without making progress, as soon as they try to enter the critical section. Wait-Free Objects Definition Given a set of processes J = {J 1 , . . . n } wishing to access a shared object S, the implementation of S is wait-free if: each process J i ∈ J must complete an operation after taking a finite number of steps.
Guarantees that all non-halted processes will make progress, regardless of the execution speed of other processes.
The wait-free condition is strictly stronger than the lock-free condition. Lock-Free Versus Wait-Free
Lock-free and wait-free objects are not (and cannot be) based on critical sections and locks.
Lock-free objects are typically implemented using retry loops are potentially unbounded and may give rise to starvation for some processes.
Wait-freedom precludes all waiting dependencies among processes, including potentially unbounded loops.
Individual wait-free operations are therefore necessarily starvation-free.

For instance, if a write to v does not involve writing v j , we pretend that a write to v j (which did not change its value) was performed.

If v is not a single digit, reading and writing it may involve a sequence of separate operations.
These operations take a certain amount of time any may overlap with each other.

In this example, the "green" read will return v [2] .

On the other hand, a read of v which is performed concurrently (and overlaps) with one or more writes to v may obtain a value different from any v [i] .
Intuitively, the value may contain "traces" of different versions.

div.head: If a read obtains traces of v
div.p: , we say that it obtained a value of v [k ,l] , where k = min(i 1 , . . . i m ) and l = max(i 1 , . . . i m ). It must be 0 ≤ k ≤ l.
In this example, we may be convinced that the "red" read may return traces of v [2] , v [3] , v [4] , and v [5] .
Lock-based techniques do not have this problem because they enforce mutual exclusion between read and write operations.
When using a lock-based technique, the "red" situation shown in the example simply cannot happen.

div.head: Properties of the Reads Theorem
div.p: Let v = d 1 , . . . d m be an m-digit number, and assume that i ≤ j implies v [i] ≤ v [j] .
The following propositions hold: A reader can access the shared data while they are being written and obtain an inconsistent value.
After reading, it checks whether it might have obtained an inconsistent value.
If this is the case, it retries the operation.
Intuitively, it may happen that a reader loops for a long time if write operations are "frequent enough", so that the reader likely obtains an inconsistent value on each try.

div.head: Consistency Check
div.p: The algorithm maintains two shared, multi-digit version numbers associated with the shared data: v1 and v2. It is assumed that initially v1 = v2.
The writer increments v1 from left to right before starting to write the shared data.
Then, it increments v2 from right to left after finishing the write operation.
The reader reads v2 from left to right before starting to read.
Then, it reads v1 from right to left after finishing the read.

div.head: Definitions (I)
div.p: A concurrent system is a collection of n sequential processes.
They communicate through shared objects.
Processes are sequential, i.e. they invoke a sequence of operations on the shared objects.
Processes can halt at arbitrary points of their execution, and exhibit arbitrary variations in speed.
Objects are typed. The type of an object defines the set of its possible values, as well as the operations that can be carried out on it.
Objects are assumed to have a sequential specification that defines the object behavior when its operations are invoked sequentially by a single process.

div.head: Definitions (II)
div.p: When dealing with a concurrent system, it is necessary to give a meaning to interleaved operation executions.

An object is linearizable if each operation appears to have taken place instantaneously at some point between the invocation of the operation and its conclusion. This property implies that processes operating on a linearizable object appear to be interleaved at the granularity of complete operations. Moreover, the order of non-overlapping operations is preserved.
Linearizability is the basic correctness condition of the Herlihy's concurrent objects.

div.head: Assumptions on Objects
div.p: Shared objects are assumed to be "small", that is, they are small enough to be copied efficiently.
A sequential object occupies a fixed-size, contiguous area of memory, called a block.

div.head: Constraints on the Sequential Implementation
div.p: Any sequential operation invoked on an object cannot have any other side effect other than modifying the block occupied by the object itself.
All sequential operations must be total, that is, they must have a well-defined behavior for any legal, or consistent state of the object they are invoked on.
For example, a dequeue operation invoked on an empty queue is allowed to return an error indication, but is not allowed to execute an illegal instruction.

div.head: Memory Management
div.p: At each instant, each of the n processes owns a single block of unused memory.
The (n + 1) th block holding the current version of the object is not owned by anyone.
In step 2, the process copies the object's current version into its own block.

When the store_conditional is performed successfully in step 4, the process implicitly becomes the owner of the block that held the object's old version and relinquishes the block it owned previously.

div.head: Consequences of the Race Condition
div.p: This race condition is not harmful for the consistency of the shared object itself.
In fact, when P eventually performs its store_conditional, this operation will surely fail (because Q's store_conditional preceded it).
As a consequence, P will carry out a new update attempt.
However, it poses a significant software engineering problem.

Even if it is (relatively) easy to ensure that any operation invoked on a consistent object will not do anything nasty (execution of illegal instructions, division by zero, . . . ), this property may be extremely difficult to ensure when it is invoked on an arbitrary bit pattern.

div.head: Consistency Check
div.p: A consistency check is inserted between steps 2 and 3 of the algorithm (i.e. between the copy and the execution of the sequential operation).
If the consistency check fails, then the source object was modified during the copy.
Hence, the copied object may be inconsistent and the process must restart from step 1 without acting on it.
The consistency check can be assisted by hardware, and built upon a so-called validate instruction.
This instruction checks whether a variable previously read with load_linked has been modified or not. Both counters are unbounded and start from the same value.
Before starting to modify an object, a process increments C 0 . After finishing, it also increments C 1 .

On the other hand, C 1 and C 0 are read before starting and after finishing to copy an object, respectively. The consistency check consists of comparing these values: if they match, the copied object is consistent.
As in Lamport's work, incrementing the counters in one order and reading them in the opposite order is crucial to the correctness of the algorithm.

div.head: Bounded Counters
div.p: The consistency check may succeed incorrectly if the counters are bounded and a counter cycles all the way around during a single update attempt.
The probability of this error can be made arbitrarily small by enlarging the counters.

Lamport's work on the readers/writer problem can be useful when the size of the counters exceeds the maximum data size on which the architecture can perform atomic load and store operations. Work (still) in progress. . . The basic scheme just described is quite inefficient, but it can be enhanced considerably.
The scheme can be made wait-free by means of a general technique known as operation combining.
This scheme is not suited for "large" objects, but other universal constructions have been proposed just for that case.
In general, lock and wait-free synchronization is still an active research topic, above all for what concerns its real-world implementation.
